consensus.consensusInference: The spring's dispersion has collapsed into agreement. Every major centre now carries El Niño at ~97–98% with a very-strong peak the central case — the disagreement is no longer about whether, but about how extreme. ECMWF sits at the aggressive extreme (anomalies possibly above +3°C, i.e. record-challenging), while NOAA's 81% very-strong figure for Oct–Dec is the more measured read; GFDL's July ensemble has all 30 members competitive with the strongest events of the past century. When the debate shifts from 'will it happen' to 'how big is the peak,' the event itself is settled. The residual uncertainty is magnitude and timing, not direction.

timeline.inference: Read the shape carefully: this is the probability that El Niño is present in each month, not its strength. It sits near-certain (97–98%) through the second half of 2026 and only declines in spring–summer 2027 — that fall is the expected end-of-event decay, not a weakening now. El Niño events peak in NH winter and fade the following spring, and GFDL's July run explicitly projects weakening into spring 2027. Meanwhile the separate strength probability is still rising (very-strong odds went from ~25% in May to 81% for Oct–Dec). So both hold at once: near-certain to persist through 2026, increasingly likely to peak very strong, and expected to decay through 2027.
